item.text: {"text":"HSTU was introduced for nonstationary recommendation sequences in [Actions Speak Louder than Words (ICML 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152); its architecture alone does not establish whether a fitted model captures current intent. [Robust Training of Sequential Recommender Systems with Missing Input Data (2024)](https://iris.uniroma1.it/bitstream/11573/1740238/1/Siciliano_Robust-Training_2024.pdf) reports strong ranking sensitivity to removing recent interactions and evaluates changes beyond aggregate accuracy. [Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) also cautions that excessive emphasis on recent items can hurt recommendation performance. These findings motivate measuring both recency dependence and ranking stability, without assuming greater sensitivity is better.\n\nA proposed HSTU diagnostic: keep the trained model and candidate sets fixed; compare unchanged histories with recent-window truncation, valid-item shuffling, and removal of a coherent recent activity block identified from available timestamps or item text. Match deletion counts against random and older-block removals; shuffle while preserving the last item separately from shuffling all valid items to distinguish broader order effects from last-item dependence. Repack histories with left padding and read the final nonpadding position. Report paired target-rank changes, HR@10 changes, and top-10 overlap, stratified by history length. These are proposed sensitivity measurements, not published HSTU-specific findings or proof of causal preferences. [Disentangling User and Item Sequence Patterns (RecSys 2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748042) shows that shuffling can confound user behavior with item availability, reinforcing the need for cautious interpretation and temporal controls."}
